stem: Unauthorized people keep following badged employees through a secure door (tailgating). Which control BEST prevents this?

options.text: A mantrap / access-control vestibule that admits one person at a time
options.rationale: A mantrap (access-control vestibule) uses interlocking doors to allow only one person through at a time, directly defeating tailgating/piggybacking.
Lighting improves visibility but does not physically prevent someone from following through the door.
Ceiling height has no effect on tailgating.
A chime does not stop an unauthorized person from entering behind an employee.

stem: A data center needs fire suppression that will not destroy its electronics. Which suppression type is BEST?

options.text: A clean-agent/gas system (e.g., FM-200 or inert gas)
options.rationale: Clean-agent gas systems suppress fire without water damage to electronics, making them ideal for computer rooms (Halon is banned; FM-200/inert gases replace it).

options.text: A standard wet-pipe water sprinkler directly over the servers
options.rationale: Water would damage the electronics; it is not preferred for computer rooms.
Halon is banned due to ozone depletion; modern clean agents replace it.
Omitting suppression leaves a fire unchecked, endangering people and equipment.

stem: An electrical fire ignites in a server rack. This is MOST accurately which fire class, and what agent is appropriate?

options.text: Class C — use a non-conductive agent (e.g., CO2 or clean agent), not water
options.rationale: Electrical fires are Class C and require a non-conductive suppression agent to avoid electrocution and equipment damage.
Class A is ordinary combustibles; using water on an energized electrical fire is dangerous.
Class K is for cooking oils, not electrical equipment.

options.text: Class D — use dry metal powder
options.rationale: Class D is combustible metals, not electrical equipment.

stem: A facility must ride through both brief power blips and multi-hour outages. Which combination MOST appropriately addresses both?

options.text: A UPS for short outages/clean power plus a generator for extended outages
options.rationale: A UPS covers brief interruptions and conditions power, while a generator sustains operations through long outages beyond battery runtime.

options.text: A UPS alone for all multi-hour outages
options.rationale: UPS batteries are for short durations; extended outages require a generator.

options.text: A generator alone with no UPS
options.rationale: Generators take time to start; a UPS is needed to bridge that gap and clean the power.
Emergency lighting does not power the facility's equipment.

stem: In power terminology, a 'brownout' refers to which of the following?

options.rationale: A brownout is a sustained reduction in voltage, distinct from a momentary sag or a full blackout.
That describes a spike/surge, not a brownout.

options.text: A complete prolonged loss of power
options.rationale: That is a blackout, not a brownout.

options.text: A momentary complete loss of power
options.rationale: That is a fault, not a brownout.

stem: Why is positive air pressure MOST desirable in a sensitive equipment room?

options.text: Air flows outward, keeping smoke, dust, and contaminants from entering when doors open
options.rationale: Positive pressure pushes air out, preventing contaminants and smoke from being drawn into the protected space.

options.text: It pulls outside air and contaminants inward
options.rationale: That describes negative pressure, which would draw contaminants in — the opposite of the goal.

options.text: It makes the room colder than absolute zero
options.rationale: This is physically nonsensical and unrelated to pressure's purpose.

options.text: It increases humidity to cause condensation
options.rationale: Condensation is undesirable; positive pressure is about keeping contaminants out, not raising humidity.

stem: A server room's humidity is far too low. What is the MOST likely resulting risk?

options.text: Static electricity discharge that can damage electronic components
options.rationale: Low humidity increases static buildup, and electrostatic discharge can harm sensitive electronics.
Condensation results from high humidity, not low humidity.
Overly dry air introduces static risk; it is not a benign condition.
Low humidity does not trigger fire suppression.

stem: To prevent a vehicle from ramming through a building entrance, which control is BEST?

options.text: Bollards (sturdy vehicle barriers) at the entrance
options.rationale: Bollards are designed to stop vehicles from ramming a building or protected area.
A mat provides no vehicle-stopping protection.
Signage may warn but does not physically stop a vehicle.
A flagpole is not a vehicle barrier.

stem: A computer area wants a water-based system that reduces accidental discharge risk by requiring both a detector and a sprinkler head to activate before water flows. Which system is BEST?

options.rationale: Preaction systems keep pipes dry and require both detection and head activation before releasing water, reducing accidental water damage risk in sensitive areas.

options.text: A wet-pipe system always full of water
options.rationale: Wet-pipe pipes are always charged, increasing accidental-discharge risk near electronics.

options.text: A deluge system that opens all heads at once
options.rationale: Deluge floods the whole area immediately, unsuitable for reducing accidental discharge in a computer room.
Omitting suppression is unsafe; a preaction system meets the stated goal.

stem: Before a gas-based suppression system discharges in an occupied room, what should FIRST occur to protect people?

options.text: An alarm/pre-discharge warning with time for occupants to evacuate safely
options.rationale: Occupants must be alerted and given time to evacuate before a gas agent discharges, since life safety takes precedence over equipment protection.
Discharging without warning could endanger occupants, violating life-safety priority.

options.text: Locking occupants in to contain the agent
options.rationale: Trapping people endangers life and is never acceptable.
Blocking exits prevents safe evacuation, violating life safety.

stem: A legacy computer room still uses a Halon fire-suppression system. What is the MOST accurate concern?

options.text: Halon is banned as an ozone-depleting substance and should be replaced with a modern clean agent
options.rationale: Halon production is banned due to ozone depletion; replacements like FM-200 or inert gases are used instead.

options.text: Halon is the safest and most modern option available
options.rationale: Halon is outdated and banned; it is not the modern option.
Halon is a gaseous agent, not water-based.

options.text: Halon must be sprayed directly on people
options.rationale: Suppression agents are not applied to people, and this misrepresents the concern (which is the ozone ban).

stem: A kitchen grease fire ignites. This is MOST accurately which fire class?

options.rationale: Cooking oil/grease fires are Class K, requiring wet chemical suppression designed for kitchens.
Class C is electrical fires, not cooking oils.
Grease fires are Class K, not ordinary combustibles.
Class D is combustible metals, not cooking oils.

stem: To deter determined intruders at a perimeter, which fence specification is MOST appropriate?

options.text: An ~8-foot fence topped with barbed/razor wire
options.rationale: Roughly 8 feet with barbed wire is guidance for deterring determined intruders, versus lower fences that only deter casual trespass.
A very low fence deters only casual entry, not determined intruders.
No perimeter barrier offers no deterrence or delay.

options.text: A painted line on the ground
options.rationale: A painted line provides no physical barrier.

stem: Which suppression choice is LEAST appropriate directly over energized computer equipment?

options.text: A wet-pipe water sprinkler discharging onto the equipment
options.rationale: Water on energized electronics risks equipment damage and shock, making it the least appropriate direct choice for a computer room.
Clean agents suppress fire without water damage, appropriate for electronics.
CO2 is non-conductive and can be appropriate for electrical fires with proper safety measures.

options.text: A preaction system reducing accidental discharge
options.rationale: Preaction reduces accidental water release, more appropriate than a wet-pipe system in sensitive areas.

stem: What is the PRIMARY function of a UPS in a facility?

options.text: To provide immediate battery-backed, conditioned power during brief outages and voltage disturbances
options.rationale: A UPS supplies clean, uninterrupted power for short outages and smooths voltage fluctuations, bridging to a generator if needed.

options.text: To permanently power the facility for weeks
options.rationale: UPS batteries are short-duration; extended power needs a generator.
A UPS is a power device, not an encryption tool.
A UPS provides power, not fire suppression.

stem: Relying solely on standard pin-tumbler locks for a high-security area is risky MOST because of which weakness?

options.text: They can be picked or bumped, so they should be layered with other controls
options.rationale: Mechanical locks are vulnerable to picking/bumping; high-security areas need layered controls (guards, access systems, monitoring).
Standard mechanical locks do not require electricity; the concern is picking/bumping.
Standard locks do not auto-unlock; that is not their inherent weakness.
Locks do not encrypt; the weakness is mechanical bypass.

stem: Installing monitored CCTV throughout a facility MOST directly supports which combination of objectives?

options.text: Detection and deterrence (and evidence for response)
options.rationale: Visible CCTV deters, and monitored/recorded footage detects incidents and supports investigation/response.
CCTV monitors; it does not suppress fires.
CCTV is unrelated to power conditioning.
CCTV is a physical monitoring control, not a data-encryption mechanism.

stem: To protect equipment from momentary high-voltage spikes, which control is BEST?

options.text: Surge protection / line conditioning (often built into a UPS)
options.rationale: Surge protectors and line conditioners absorb voltage spikes to protect equipment; UPS units commonly include this.
Fire extinguishers address fire, not electrical spikes.
Lighting does not protect against voltage spikes.
An alarm does not condition or protect against power spikes.

stem: Compared with purely automated controls, what is the MOST distinctive advantage of using human security guards?

options.text: Discretionary judgment to assess unusual situations and respond flexibly
options.rationale: Guards can exercise judgment and adapt to novel or ambiguous situations in ways fixed automated controls cannot.

options.text: They never need training or rest
options.rationale: Guards require training and rest; this is a limitation, not an advantage.

options.text: They are always cheaper than any technology
options.rationale: Guards are often more costly than automation; cost is not their distinctive advantage.
Guards are a physical control and do not encrypt data.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant to protecting a data center's physical environment?

options.text: The brand of the office wall clock
options.rationale: A wall clock's brand has no bearing on physical environmental protection, making it least relevant.
Fire controls are essential to environmental protection.
UPS/generator power protection is critical to a data center.
HVAC control protects equipment and is highly relevant.
